title: What training do psychosocial hazard regulations expect?
description: What the WHS psychosocial regulations and Victoria's 2025 Psychological Health Regulations expect of training, where it fits as a control, and what to record.
shortAnswer: Australian psychosocial hazard regulations require employers to eliminate or minimise risks from hazards such as bullying, harassment, high job demands and traumatic exposure. Training is expected, but as a supporting control: the model WHS Regulations list training as a matter to consider, and Victoria's Psychological Health Regulations 2025 allow information, instruction or training to be relied on alone only where changing work design, systems or environment is not reasonably practicable.
keyTakeaways: Model WHS Regulations 55A to 55D define psychosocial hazards and risks and require PCBUs to manage them using the hierarchy of controls.
Regulation 55D(2)(i) lists information, training, instruction and supervision as a relevant matter when choosing controls; in the Commonwealth these rules have applied since 1 April 2023.
Victoria's Occupational Health and Safety (Psychological Health) Regulations 2025 commenced on 1 December 2025 and restrict reliance on information, instruction or training.
Safe Work Australia's model code expects supervisors and managers to be trained to respond to harmful behaviours, and workers to demonstrate competence rather than simply acknowledge procedures.
Training records should show which psychosocial risk each training activity supports and which higher order control it sits alongside.
jurisdiction: Australia: Commonwealth and model WHS jurisdictions (as adopted locally); Victoria under the OHS (Psychological Health) Regulations 2025
regulator: Safe Work Australia (model laws and code); Comcare and state and territory WHS regulators; WorkSafe Victoria
appliesTo: Persons conducting a business or undertaking (PCBUs) in model WHS jurisdictions
Officers, managers and supervisors with responsibility for work design and people
Workers exposed to psychosocial hazards, including those in customer facing and trauma exposed roles

sections.heading: What do the psychosocial hazard regulations require?

blocks.text: The regulations require PCBUs to manage psychosocial risks in the same way as physical risks: identify the hazards, eliminate the risk if reasonably practicable, and otherwise minimise it using the hierarchy of controls. Training is part of the control picture, not a substitute for it. This page describes the position as at September 2026.

In the Commonwealth [Work Health and Safety Regulations 2011](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2011L02664/latest/text), Division 11 of Part 3.1 contains four provisions. Regulation 55A defines a psychosocial hazard as a hazard that arises from or relates to the design or management of work, the work environment, plant at a workplace, or workplace interactions or behaviours, and that may cause psychological harm. Regulation 55B defines psychosocial risk. Regulation 55C requires a PCBU to manage psychosocial risks in accordance with Part 3.1 and implement the control measures required by regulation 55D.

Regulation 55D(2) lists the matters a PCBU must have regard to when choosing controls. They include the duration, frequency and severity of exposure; how hazards interact; the design of work, including job demands and tasks; systems of work; the workplace layout and environment; workplace interactions or behaviours; and, at paragraph (i), "the information, training, instruction and supervision provided to workers".

These provisions were added to the Commonwealth Regulations by an amendment registered as F2023L00012, and the psychosocial items commenced on 1 April 2023. [Comcare's regulatory guide](https://www.comcare.gov.au/scheme-legislation/whs-act/regulatory-guides/managing-psychosocial-hazards) also refers to the Work Health and Safety (Managing Psychosocial Hazards at Work) Code of Practice 2024 for the Commonwealth jurisdiction. Other model law jurisdictions adopted equivalent regulations on their own timetables, so check the local regulator for commencement and code status.

sections.heading: Where does training fit in controlling psychosocial risks?

blocks.text: Training is a supporting control. It helps workers and supervisors apply higher order controls, such as changes to workload, rostering, role clarity or reporting systems, but training alone rarely eliminates a psychosocial hazard that comes from how work is designed.

Safe Work Australia's [model Code of Practice: Managing psychosocial hazards at work](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/doc/model-code-practice-managing-psychosocial-hazards-work) (published August 2022) describes administrative controls and personal protective equipment as the least reliable controls, and says a PCBU must consider what information, training, instruction or supervision is needed to make chosen controls effective. The code must be approved in a jurisdiction to have legal effect there, but it is the reference point regulators use.

blocks.title: Model code on training standard
blocks.text: "Training should require workers to demonstrate they are competent in performing the task. It is not sufficient to simply tell a worker about the procedure and ask them to acknowledge they understand and can perform it." Safe Work Australia, Managing psychosocial hazards at work: Code of Practice.

The code gives a specific example for leaders: if supervisors and managers have a role in implementing policies on harmful behaviours, the PCBU must provide the training needed for them to know what to do if they witness or receive a report of violence and aggression, bullying or sexual harassment. It also says information and training must be in a form all workers can understand, which may mean other languages.

sections.heading: How do Victoria's Psychological Health Regulations treat training?

blocks.text: Victoria goes further than the model regulations by legally ranking training below changes to work. The Occupational Health and Safety (Psychological Health) Regulations 2025 (S.R. No. 103/2025) came into operation on 1 December 2025, and regulation 15 sets out how Victorian employers must control psychosocial risks.

items: Regulation 15(1): the employer must, so far as is reasonably practicable, eliminate any risk associated with a psychosocial hazard.

Regulation 15(2): if elimination is not reasonably practicable, the employer must reduce the risk by altering the management of work, plant, systems of work, work design or the workplace environment; or by using information, instruction or training; or a combination.
Regulation 15(3): the employer may only use information, instruction or training exclusively if none of the alterations in 15(2)(a) are reasonably practicable.
Regulation 15(4): where a combination is used, information, instruction or training must not be the predominant control measure.

blocks.text: Regulation 16 requires employers to review and, if necessary, revise controls, including before changes likely to affect psychosocial risks, when new information becomes available, and when a psychological injury or psychosocial hazard is reported. For training teams, that means content supporting psychosocial controls needs a review trigger tied to those events. [WorkSafe Victoria](https://www.worksafe.vic.gov.au/news/2025-12/new-regulations-make-psychological-health-priority) has published a compliance code alongside the regulations.

The general Victorian training duty in section 21(2)(e) of the OHS Act 2004 still applies. The comparison with the model laws is covered in [the WHS Act duty to provide training](/regulations/whs-act-duty-to-provide-training).

sections.heading: Who needs psychosocial hazard training, and what should it cover?

blocks.text: Training needs differ by role, because each group controls different parts of the risk. The table below is an illustrative starting point drawn from the matters in regulation 55D and the model code; it is not a prescribed curriculum.

blocks.caption: Illustrative mapping: role to training focus to evidence
head: Role
Training focus
Evidence that it worked
rows: Duty to manage psychosocial risk, reading risk data, resourcing work design changes
Board papers show psychosocial risks, controls and review dates; officer briefing records
Recognising hazards such as high job demands or poor role clarity; responding to reports of bullying, harassment or aggression; when to escalate
Scenario based assessment of response to a report; supervisor sign off on the reporting procedure version
What the organisation's psychosocial controls are, how to report hazards and harmful behaviour, where to get support
Knowledge check on reporting channels; engagement survey items on awareness
Customer facing or trauma exposed roles
Specific procedures for aggression, de escalation, debriefing and exposure to distressing content
Practical scenario assessment; record of debrief procedure training linked to the risk assessment
Handling reports confidentially, trauma informed practice, record keeping
Observed or simulated complaint handling assessed against the procedure

blocks.text: Sexual harassment is both a psychosocial hazard under WHS laws and conduct covered by the positive duty in the Sex Discrimination Act, so the two training programs should be designed together. See [positive duty sexual harassment training](/regulations/positive-duty-sexual-harassment-training).

sections.heading: What records show psychosocial training obligations are met?

blocks.text: Good records connect each training activity to a named psychosocial risk and to the higher order control it supports. That link is what shows a regulator the training was chosen as part of risk management, rather than as a stand alone response.

items: The psychosocial risk assessment, with the training activity listed against each relevant risk and control.
Training content with a version date, so it can be matched to the procedure and risk assessment in force at the time.
Competency evidence for supervisors and complaint handlers, such as scenario assessments, not only attendance.
Review records showing when content was updated after a change, a report or new information (the Victorian regulation 16 triggers are a useful checklist even outside Victoria).
Consultation records showing workers and health and safety representatives were involved in choosing controls, including training.

blocks.text: The model code notes that record keeping can show how risks were assessed, which controls were implemented and what training was provided. For the mechanics, see [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) and [how to evidence training effectiveness to a regulator](/guides/how-to-evidence-training-effectiveness-to-a-regulator).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records each psychosocial risk, its controls and the learning outcomes that support those controls as linked items, so training can be traced back to the risk assessment it serves. Assessment points are defined per role, and a change to a procedure or risk rating flags the dependent training for review. See [knowledge governance](/platform/knowledge-governance).

faqs.q: Is mental health awareness training enough to comply with psychosocial regulations?
faqs.a: Usually not on its own. The regulations require psychosocial risks to be eliminated or minimised through the hierarchy of controls, and Safe Work Australia's code treats administrative controls as the least reliable. In Victoria, information, instruction or training can be the only control only if altering work design, systems or environment is not reasonably practicable, and must not be the predominant control in a combination.

faqs.q: Do the psychosocial regulations prescribe specific courses?
faqs.a: No. Neither the model WHS Regulations nor the Victorian regulations prescribe a course, duration or refresher interval. Training must be suitable and adequate for the work, the risks and the controls under regulation 39 of the model Regulations, which means content is driven by the organisation's own psychosocial risk assessment.

faqs.q: When did the Victorian Psychological Health Regulations start?
faqs.a: The Occupational Health and Safety (Psychological Health) Regulations 2025 came into operation on 1 December 2025. WorkSafe Victoria has said inspectors will consider an employer's previous experience with psychosocial risk management when deciding on a compliance and enforcement response.

faqs.q: Do psychosocial rules apply to small businesses?
faqs.a: Yes. The duty applies to all PCBUs in model law jurisdictions and all employers in Victoria. What is reasonably practicable depends on the circumstances, so a small business may use simpler controls and training, but it still needs to identify psychosocial hazards and manage the risks.

factCheck.claim: Regulation 55A defines a psychosocial hazard as arising from design or management of work, work environment, plant, or workplace interactions or behaviours, that may cause psychological harm.
Regulation 55D(2)(i) lists the information, training, instruction and supervision provided to workers as a relevant matter when determining psychosocial control measures.
Psychosocial items of F2023L00012 (Sch 1 items 1 and 2) commenced in the Commonwealth Regulations on 1 April 2023 (compilation endnotes).
Comcare's regulatory guide names the Work Health and Safety (Managing Psychosocial Hazards at Work) Code of Practice 2024 as approved under the WHS Act.

Model code (publication date August 2022) states training should require workers to demonstrate competence and it is not sufficient to tell a worker about a procedure and ask them to acknowledge it; must be approved in a jurisdiction to have legal effect.
Victorian OHS (Psychological Health) Regulations 2025, S.R. No. 103/2025, come into operation on 1 December 2025 (regulation 3).

Victorian regulation 15(3) permits exclusive use of information, instruction or training only if none of the 15(2)(a) measures are reasonably practicable; 15(4) says it must not be the predominant control in a combination.

WorkSafe Victoria announced commencement on 1 December 2025, published a compliance code, and said inspectors will consider previous experience with psychosocial risk management in enforcement responses.
